headline: Gulf disabling-fire report leaves attacker and damaged hulls unresolved
deck: The day moved from broad regional claims to reported commercial hull damage, while the attacker and the link between the incidents remain unresolved.
body: Al Arabiya carried the first firm maritime gate available in the record: several merchant vessels in the northern Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman had been hit by disabling fire. The available fragment does not name the advisory speaker, identify the hulls, assign an attacker, or establish casualties or pollution. It does put commercial shipping damage on the record after a morning of regional claims that were still thinner than the traffic picture around the Gulf. [E1]

A separate report placed a tanker in trouble near the UAE, where the vessel was seen listing after a possible projectile attack. The available Record fragment supports that narrower point, not a precise distance from Port Rashid, a named master report, or a confirmed water-ingress account. That leaves the Dubai-approaches report relevant to the sequence, but not enough to specify the mechanism or tie it to the wider disabling-fire report. [E2]

The sequence matters because the earlier Iran-US tanker-attack context was broader than the confirmed maritime record. Channel NewsAsia carried the regional tanker-attack frame, but the fragment available here does not establish specific Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps counts for US hulls, tankers or Hormuz violators. The article therefore separates that background from the later commercial-shipping damage reports. [E3]

The stronger reading is that the escalation moved from regional tanker-war claims toward merchant traffic near Gulf state waters. The weaker reading is that the UAE listing and the multiple-vessel fire report may still describe partly overlapping reports, or damage whose cause is not yet established. The fact that would break the sequence is a maritime authority, flag-state or port-authority list tying named hulls, locations and damage to one incident set.

For now, the authority line is narrow. The Al Arabiya-framed report says several merchant vessels were hit by disabling fire, and a separate press report records a listing tanker near the UAE; neither assigns responsibility in the fragments carried here. The record cannot turn regional claims, OSINT reports or rumors into attribution. [E1] [E2]

That leaves the escalation visible but incomplete. Commercial hulls were damaged or in distress across the northern Arabian Gulf, Gulf of Oman and UAE approaches, and the war-risk question has moved onto ordinary merchant traffic. What still stands at filing is the order of the record: the disabling-fire report, the UAE listing beside it, commercial hull damage in the first account, and responsibility still unresolved. [E1] [E2]
